title: Binding Energy
lead: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy needed to pull it apart into separate protons and neutrons, and it can be found from atomic masses. How the binding energy per nucleon changes from the lightest nuclei to the heaviest tells how the nuclear force and the Coulomb force together decide which nuclei are most tightly bound.
objectives: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of a particle.
summary_html: • The binding energy (BE) of a nucleus is the energy needed to separate it into individual protons and neutrons. In terms of atomic masses, $$\kBE = \{[Zm({}^{1}\text{H}) + N\kmn] - m({}^{A}\text{X})\}\kc^{2},$$ where $m({}^{1}\text{H})$ is the mass of a hydrogen atom, $m({}^{A}\text{X})$ is the atomic mass of the nuclide, and $\kmn$ is the mass of a neutron. Patterns in the binding energy per nucleon, $\kBE/A$, reveal details of the nuclear force. The larger the $\kBE/A$, the more stable the nucleus.

figures.original_caption: Work done to pull a nucleus apart into its constituent protons and neutrons increases the mass of the system. The work to disassemble the nucleus equals its binding energy BE. A bound system has less mass than the sum of its parts, especially noticeable in the nuclei, where forces and energies are very large.

The center of the Earth cools by well-known heat transfer methods. Convection in the liquid regions and conduction move thermal energy to the surface, where it radiates into cold, dark space. Given the age of the Earth and its initial temperature, it should have cooled to a lower temperature by now. The blowup shows that nuclear decay releases energy in the Earth’s interior. This energy has slowed the cooling process and is responsible for the interior still being molten.

(Figure 31.24) A graph of average binding energy per nucleon, BE/A, for stable nuclei. The most tightly bound nuclei are those with A near 60, where the attractive nuclear force has its greatest effect. At higher A s, the Coulomb repulsion progressively reduces the binding energy per nucleon, because the nuclear force is short ranged. The spikes on the curve are very tightly bound nuclides and indicate shell closures. (Figure 31.25) The nuclear force is attractive and stronger than the Coulomb force, but it is short ranged. In low-mass nuclei, each nucleon feels the nuclear attraction of all others. In larger nuclei, the range of the nuclear force, shown for a single nucleon, is smaller than the size of the nucleus, but the Coulomb repulsion from all protons reaches all others. If the nucleus is large enough, the Coulomb repulsion can add to overcome the nuclear attraction.

exercises.prompt: Binding energy is a measure of how much work must be done against nuclear forces in order to disassemble a nucleus into its constituent parts. For example, the amount of energy in order to disassemble ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ into 2 protons and 2 neutrons requires 28.3 MeV of work to be done on the nuclear particles. Describe the force that makes it so difficult to pull a nucleus apart. Would it be accurate to say that the electric force plays a role in the forces within a nucleus? Explain why or why not.

answer.solution: The force that holds a nucleus together is the strong nuclear force. It attracts every nucleon to its neighbors, protons and neutrons alike, and is about 100 times stronger than the Coulomb force, but it acts only over a short range, about the size of a nucleus. Pulling ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ apart means doing work against this attraction, which is why 28.3 MeV is needed. The electric force does play a role, so it would be accurate to say so: the two protons repel each other by the Coulomb force, which acts inside the nucleus as it does anywhere else. It works against the binding rather than for it, and at nuclear distances it is much weaker than the nuclear attraction, so the nucleus stays bound. In heavy nuclei the Coulomb repulsion of many protons adds up while the short-ranged nuclear attraction does not, and this lowers the binding energy per nucleon.

exercises.prompt: Why is the number of neutrons greater than the number of protons in stable nuclei having $A$ greater than about 40, and why is this effect more pronounced for the heaviest nuclei?

answer.solution: Every proton repels every other proton by the Coulomb force, which is long ranged, while the nuclear attraction acts only between near neighbors and acts on neutrons as well as protons. A neutron added to a nucleus adds nuclear attraction with its neighbors but no repulsion, and it keeps the protons farther apart. In a small nucleus the repulsion is weak and $Z \approx N$ is most stable, but the total Coulomb repulsion grows roughly as $Z^2$, since each proton repels all the others, while the nuclear attraction grows only in proportion to $A$. Beyond about $A = 40$ stability therefore needs extra neutrons, and the heavier the nucleus the more the repulsion outgrows the attraction, so the excess of neutrons is largest for the heaviest nuclei.

exercises.prompt: Explain how a bound system can have less mass than its components. Why is this not observed classically, say for a building made of bricks?

answer.solution: To separate a bound system into its parts, work must be done on it, and that energy appears as extra rest mass of the separated parts, $\kdm = \kBE/\kc^{2}$. Put the other way, when the parts come together and bind, the binding energy is released and the bound system is left with that much less rest energy, so it has less mass than its parts by $\kBE/\kc^{2}$. The same is true of a building of bricks held by mortar and gravity, but the binding energies there are chemical and gravitational energies of a few eV per atom or less, while the rest energy of each atom is billions of eV. The mass difference is a fraction of about $10^{-10}$ or smaller, far too small to measure. Only in nuclei, where binding energies are millions of electron volts per nucleon, is it large enough to see.

exercises.prompt: Spontaneous radioactive decay occurs only when the decay products have less mass than the parent, and it tends to produce a daughter that is more stable than the parent. Explain how this is related to the fact that more tightly bound nuclei are more stable. (Consider the binding energy per nucleon.)

answer.solution: A more tightly bound nucleus has a larger binding energy per nucleon, $\kBE/A$, and so a larger mass defect for its number of nucleons: its nucleons have given up more rest energy in binding. A decay keeps the number of nucleons fixed, so it can lower the mass only by rearranging the nucleons into a more tightly bound daughter and products, with a greater total binding energy. The mass that disappears is released as the kinetic energy of the products, and a decay that would raise the mass cannot happen spontaneously. Spontaneous decay therefore runs from less tightly bound to more tightly bound nuclei, that is, toward larger $\kBE/A$, which is toward greater stability.

exercises.prompt: To obtain the most precise value of BE from the equation $\text{BE}=[ZM({}^{1}\text{H})+Nm_{n}]c^{2}-m({}^{A}\text{X})c^{2}$, we should take into account the binding energy of the electrons in the neutral atoms. Will doing this produce a larger or smaller value for BE? Why is this effect usually negligible?

answer.solution: Each atomic mass is less than the mass of its nucleus and its free electrons by the binding energy of those electrons divided by $c^2$. In $Zm({}^{1}\text{H})$ each hydrogen atom is short by only 13.6 eV, but the atom ${}^{A}\text{X}$, with $Z$ electrons, many of them tightly bound in inner shells, is short by more than $Z$ times 13.6 eV. Its mass is therefore lowered more, which makes the bracket in the equation, and so $\text{BE}$, come out too large. Taking the electrons' binding energy into account gives a smaller value for $\text{BE}$. The effect is usually negligible because electron binding energies are eV to tens of keV, while nuclear binding energies are millions of eV, so the correction is a few hundredths of a percent at most.

exercises.prompt: How does the finite range of the nuclear force relate to the fact that $\kBE/A$ is greatest for $A$ near 60?

answer.solution: The nuclear force reaches only about the diameter of a nucleus with $A$ near 60. In nuclei smaller than that, every nucleon is within range of every other, so each added nucleon is attracted by all the rest and $\kBE/A$ rises with $A$. In larger nuclei, an added nucleon is out of reach of the nucleons on the far side and is bound only by its neighbors, so the nuclear attraction per nucleon stops growing. The Coulomb repulsion between protons is long ranged and keeps growing with the number of protons, so beyond $A$ near 60 it lowers $\kBE/A$. The two trends meet near $A = 60$, where $\kBE/A$ is greatest.

exercises.prompt: ${}^{2}\text{H}$ is a loosely bound isotope of hydrogen. Called deuterium or heavy hydrogen, it is stable but relatively rare—it is 0.015% of natural hydrogen. Note that deuterium has $Z=N$, which should tend to make it more tightly bound, but both are odd numbers. Calculate $\kBE/A$, the binding energy per nucleon, for ${}^{2}\text{H}$ and compare it with the approximate value obtained from the graph in Figure 31.24.

answer.hint: Use $\kBE = \{[Zm({}^{1}\text{H}) + N\kmn] - m({}^{A}\text{X})\}\kc^{2}$ with $Z = N = 1$ and $m({}^{2}\text{H}) = 2.014102\;\text{u}$ from Appendix A, then divide by $A = 2$.

exercises.prompt: ${}^{209}\text{Bi}$ is the heaviest stable nuclide, and its $\kBE/A$ is low compared with medium-mass nuclides. Calculate $\kBE/A$, the binding energy per nucleon, for ${}^{209}\text{Bi}$ and compare it with the approximate value obtained from the graph in Figure 31.24.

answer.hint: Bismuth has $Z = 83$, so $N = 126$; take $m({}^{209}\text{Bi}) = 208.980374\;\text{u}$ from Appendix A, find $\kBE$ and divide by 209.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate $\kBE/A$ for ${}^{12}\text{C}$. Stable and relatively tightly bound, this nuclide is most of natural carbon. (b) Calculate $\kBE/A$ for ${}^{14}\text{C}$. Is the difference in $\kBE/A$ between ${}^{12}\text{C}$ and ${}^{14}\text{C}$ significant? One is stable and common, and the other is unstable and rare.

answer.solution:
(a) 7.680 MeV, consistent with graph
(b) 7.520 MeV, consistent with graph. Not significantly different from value for ${}^{12}\text{C}$, but sufficiently lower to allow decay into another nuclide that is more tightly bound.

exercises.prompt: The purpose of this problem is to show in three ways that the binding energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom is negligible compared with the masses of the proton and electron. (a) Calculate the mass equivalent in u of the 13.6-eV binding energy of an electron in a hydrogen atom, and compare this with the mass of the hydrogen atom obtained from Appendix A. (b) Subtract the mass of the proton given in Table 31.2 from the mass of the hydrogen atom given in Appendix A. You will find the difference is equal to the electron’s mass to three digits, implying the binding energy is small in comparison. (c) Take the ratio of the binding energy of the electron (13.6 eV) to the energy equivalent of the electron’s mass (0.511 MeV). (d) Discuss how your answers confirm the stated purpose of this problem.

parts.hint: Convert 13.6 eV to MeV and divide by 931.5 MeV/u.
Write both energies in eV before dividing.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results A particle physicist discovers a neutral particle with a mass of 2.02733 u that he assumes is two neutrons bound together. (a) Find the binding energy. (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) What assumptions are unreasonable or inconsistent?

answer.hint: Two free neutrons have mass $2\kmn = 2.017330\;\text{u}$; the binding energy is the difference from 2.02733 u times 931.5 MeV/u.
answer.solution:
(a) $-9.315\;\text{MeV}$
(b) The negative binding energy implies an unbound system.
(c) This assumption that it is two bound neutrons is incorrect.
